title: The Prevalence and Impact of Fake News on COVID-19 Vaccination in Taiwan: Retrospective Study of Digital Media
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. The paper does report shares of news items labelled 'fake news' with explicit denominators (193,188/512,435 = 37.7% during the public vaccination stage; 99,791/278,748 = 35.8% before it; weekly mean 37.4%), but the label is not a veracity judgement. 'In this study, fake news was set as news with a suspicion score greater than zero', and the suspicion score comes from the Islander system's style-based RoBERTa model trained on the Chinese valence-arousal text data set plus 198 news items labelled by two journalism experts for 'the bias of the title and objective statements or subjective claims'. The authors state the approach explicitly: 'we employed a style-based approach to fake news detection', and in the Implications section, 'While the Islander system cannot directly detect false information, it can monitor the media in real time and provide objective scores.' A wholly true article written in a sensational or subjective style therefore receives the label, which is the governing test for QUALITY rather than CONTENT; the extremely lenient threshold (any suspicion score above zero on a 0-1000 scale where zero was the modal value) is consistent with the implausibly high 37% figure. Since every share the paper reports rests on this instrument, it is a quality-only study and is excluded. NOTE FOR ADJUDICATION: if the review decides that a style-based automated 'fake news' classifier counts as veracity coding (ground_truth = classifier), the two stage-specific shares and the weekly summary statistics recorded in missed_or_uncertain below are the rows that would follow.
missed_or_uncertain: Values seen but not extracted, with their verbatim support, in case the construct call is overturned on adjudication. (1) 'A higher percentage of fake news (193,188/512,435, 37.7%; 95% CI 37.6%-37.8%) was found during the public vaccination stage, than during the nonpublic vaccination stage (99,791/278,748, 35.8%; 95% CI 35.6%-36.0%); and 11 of the 26 news media sources had significantly increased fake news percentages during the public vaccination stage' (Results, p. 5). Denominator: 791,183 COVID-19 and vaccine news items crawled from 26 Taiwanese internet news media sources, filtered by 21 Chinese/English COVID and vaccine keywords out of 2,018,278 collected items, 1 March - 25 December 2021. (2) Table 1 weekly summary over the 28-week regression window: 'Fake news (%) ... 37.4 (1.9)' mean (SD), minimum 33.7, median 37.6, maximum 41.3. (3) Two short-window figures in the Discussion: '(26,447/73,669, 35.9%; 95% CI 35.6%-36.3%)' for the two weeks after the 15 May 2021 community-spread announcement, '(19,969/52,276, 38.2%; 95% CI 37.8%-38.6%)' for the first ten days of June 2021, and August 2021 at '38.5% (95% CI 38.2%-38.8%)'. (4) The Johnson-Neyman threshold of 39.3% and the 37.4% zero-crossing point are regression thresholds on the same variable, not prevalence estimates. Nothing here is a share of consumption, of people, or of shares, so even on a reversed call the paper would yield CONTENT rows only. Also not extracted: the incitement score (mean 488.7, SD 2.4) — a continuous style score with no share; and the regression coefficients (beta=0.98 for vaccine availability, beta=-3.21 for the fake news x Google Trends interaction), which are effect estimates, not prevalence.

rob.design: Retrospective ecological study of Taiwan, 1 March - 25 December 2021, with the regression window 13 June - 25 December 2021 (28 weeks; 70/30 train/validation split at 30 October 2021). News crawled in real time by the Islander system from 26 Taiwanese digital media sources: 2,018,278 items collected, 791,183 retained after COVID-19/vaccine keyword filtering. Each item scored for suspicion and incitement (0-1000) by a RoBERTa model trained on the Chinese valence-arousal text data set (720 texts) plus 198 mid-2019 news items labelled by two journalism experts for title bias and objective-versus-subjective statements, cross-validated between them; no accuracy, precision/recall or agreement statistic is reported for the fake-news label itself. 'Fake news' operationalised as suspicion score > 0. Google Trends (news subgroup, term 'vaccine', Taiwan) used as a propagation proxy. Vaccination and case data from Taiwan's Ministry of Health and Welfare and Our World in Data. Analysis: chi-square, stepwise multivariable linear regression with VIF checks, Johnson-Neyman procedure, in R 4.1.1. Author-declared limitations: no demographic data on vaccine recipients, and the system applies only to Chinese-language news. Conflict of interest note: the Islander system is a free service of Taiwan AI Labs, the affiliation of three co-authors.
